blocks.content: Have you ever implemented an interface… only to leave half the methods empty because your class simply didn't need them?
Or added one method to a shared interface… and watched five unrelated classes break instantly?
If yes, you've likely violated the Interface Segregation Principle (ISP).
ISP is simple:
No class should be forced to implement methods it doesn't use.

ISP is the "I" in SOLID. When interfaces grow too large, they become a burden. Classes are forced to implement things they don't need, fake methods start appearing everywhere, and a single interface change ripples through your entire codebase.
This chapter covers what ISP really means, why fat interfaces cause real damage, how to split them properly, and the mistakes to avoid along the way.
Let's start with a real example.
1. The Problem: A Fat Interface
Imagine you are building a smart home system that controls different types of devices:
["Basic devices (lights, fans)","Advanced devices (smart TVs, security cameras)"]
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245771943-a6c8667e.png

All seven methods crammed into one interface. Every class is forced to implement everything even methods it will never use.SmartLightends up with four broken or empty methods just to satisfy the compiler.
You might start with what feels like a convenient design: a single unified interface that handles everything.
At first, this seems efficient. One interface, all capabilities. But as your system grows, problems start to show.
Let's say you want to create a simple smart light, a class that should only handle turning on, off, and adjusting brightness:

Even thoughSmartLightonly needs three methods, it is forced to implement four completely unrelated security and streaming capabilities. You either throw exceptions or write empty methods. Neither is a good outcome.
2. What's Wrong With This?
Interface Pollution
The SmartDevice interface is doing too much. It combines multiple unrelated responsibilities: basic device control, content streaming, security recording, and motion detection.
Any class that implements this interface must carry the weight of all seven methods even when it only needs three. This is what's known as a "fat" or "polluted" interface.
Fragile Code

Now imagine you add a new method like enableFaceRecognition(). Suddenly, all existing implementations smart lights, fans, TVs must be updated. A simple feature addition for security cameras forces changes across every device class in your system.
Violates Liskov Substitution

A client may expect any SmartDevice to support security alerts, but passing in a SmartLight will crash the program with an UnsupportedOperationException. That is a clear LSP violation. If a subtype cannot stand in for its base type without breaking callers, the contract is unreliable.
3. The Interface Segregation Principle (ISP)
"Clients should not be forced to depend on methods they do not use."
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245772105-c7b70f1c.png

This matters most in growing codebases. The bigger an interface gets, the more classes it drags into changes that have nothing to do with them. One new method added to a fat interface can force updates across dozens of unrelated classes.

ISP is the "I" in SOLID, introduced by Robert C. Martin. It applies to any language that supports interfaces or abstract base classes but it hits hardest in statically typed languages like Java, where the compiler demands every interface method be implemented, whether the class needs it or not.
4. Why Does ISP Matter?
1. Less Unnecessary Coupling
Focused interfaces mean classes only know about what they actually use. SmartLight has no business knowing about recordFootage() or sendSecurityAlert(). ISP makes sure it never has to.
2. Easier to Combine Capabilities

Small interfaces are like building blocks. A SecurityCamera can implement both Recordable and MotionDetectable. A SmartTV can implement both Streamable and BasicDevice. You compose exactly what you need nothing more.
3. Clearer Intent

When a class implements BasicDevice, you immediately know what it can do. When it implements a seven-method SmartDevice interface but throws exceptions on four of them, nobody knows what it actually supports. ISP makes capabilities explicit and honest.
4. Simpler Testing

Testing a class that uses a focused Recordable interface means mocking only recording methods. No stubbing out brightness controls, streaming URLs, or motion detection flags that have nothing to do with the test.
5. Prevents LSP Violations

Fat interfaces are a direct pipeline to LSP violations. When classes are forced to implement methods they don't support, UnsupportedOperationException becomes inevitable. ISP cuts the problem off at the source before broken implementations ever get written.
5. Applying ISP
Time to apply ISP and break down our bloated SmartDevice interface into focused, logical pieces.
Step 1: Define Smaller, Cohesive Interfaces
Instead of one fat SmartDevice interface, we create multiple focused ones:
Step 2: Classes Implement Only the Interfaces They Need
Now each device class implements only what it actually supports. No empty methods. No exceptions. No wasted code.
SmartLight (Basic only)
SmartTV (Basic + Streaming)
What if you need a full security camera that handles everything? It simply implements all relevant interfaces.
SecurityCamera (Basic + Security)

Each class implements only what it needs. SmartLight handles basic control. SmartTV adds streaming. SecurityCamera opts into security capabilities. No empty methods. No exceptions. No broken contracts.
6. Common Pitfalls While Applying ISP
Even with good intentions, these are the traps developers fall into most often.
1. Over-Segregating Interfaces

Creating a separate interface for every single method  Turnable, Dimmable, Alertable, Recordable  is just as bad as one fat interface. Now instead of one bloated file, you have twenty tiny ones that are equally hard to manage.
Group methods that naturally belong together. turnOn(), turnOff(), and adjustBrightness() all control the same thing  keep them in one BasicDevice interface.
2. Designing for the Implementer, Not the Client
ISP is not about making life easier for the class implementing the interface. It is about making life easier for the client using it.

Ask the right question: "What is the minimum this caller actually needs?" If a security monitoring service only needs recordFootage() and sendAlert(), it should never be forced to depend on brightness controls it will never touch.
3. Low Cohesion Inside Interfaces
Splitting a fat interface into smaller ones means nothing if those smaller interfaces still mix unrelated methods together.

Every method inside an interface should serve the same logical role. Think of an interface as a job description. If the methods don't all belong to the same job, the interface lacks cohesion and you haven't really solved the problem, just reorganized it.
7. Common Questions About ISP
"How small should my interfaces be?"
No strict rule but a simple test: if different clients need different methods from the same interface, split it. Every method in an interface should be used by every class that implements it.
"Won't lots of small interfaces add complexity?"
It adds more files, not more complexity. One focused interface is far easier to understand than one giant interface with fifteen methods. Structure on purpose beats confusion by accident.
"Should I refactor old code too?"
Yes when you spot the warning signs. Empty method bodies, frequent UnsupportedOperationException, or one interface change breaking unrelated classes. Start with the interfaces causing the most pain.
"Can a class implement multiple small interfaces?"

Absolutely that's the whole point. A SecurityCamera implementing BasicDevice and SecurityDevice is cleaner and more honest than one class forced into a seven-method interface it can only half support.
"How does ISP relate to LSP?"

They work together. ISP keeps interfaces lean and honest. LSP keeps implementations trustworthy. Fat interfaces force incomplete implementations which directly causes LSP violations. Fix ISP, and LSP becomes much easier to follow.
